tldr: We developed a whole-body control framework for humanoid robots that relies solely on footage from a torso-mounted monocular RGB camera to detect and estimate the state of fast-flying balls, dodge without falling, and reacquire the opponent without losing sight of them.
hero_caption: Overview of the proposed perception-action loop. In simulation, bounding boxes are rapidly generated via analytic geometric projection and noise injection, while YOLOv8 detections are used on the physical robot. A temporal estimator predicts relative ball position and a binary threat flag, and dodge/recovery and search/track policies drive all 29 joints across the body.
overview:
In environments where humans and robots share the same space, unexpected flying or falling objects pose a constant danger during ongoing tasks. When facing sudden threats, humanoids must rapidly move their entire body to dodge and immediately recover to a task-ready posture without losing balance. For a bipedal robot, successfully avoiding a ball is still a complete failure if it ends in a fall.

To tackle this, the authors turned to dodgeball as a benchmark task for agile evasion. However, relying purely on a single onboard monocular RGB camera—without external motion capture or expensive event cameras—presents steep challenges. As the robot twists its body to dodge, the camera view shifts drastically, and aggressive whole-body motions introduce heavy blur that causes visual tracking to drop out.

To solve this, the authors designed a temporal estimator that infers the 3D relative ball position and an approaching threat flag from a history of monocular bounding boxes. Furthermore, they replaced simulation image rendering with analytic geometric projection to accelerate reinforcement learning, and introduced a three-stage curriculum that decouples controller acquisition from estimator training.

In experiments on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid, the system achieved an 85%+ success rate for single dodges without external tracking. It also executed a complete continuous behavioral loop: tracking the opponent, dodging a throw, reacquiring the target via full-azimuth search, and dodging the next throw.
contributions: Proposed an analytic sphere projection method that bypasses image rendering to drastically accelerate training, along with perception randomization that mimics real-world detector noise.
Developed a temporal estimator that jointly predicts the ball's 3D relative position and a binary threat flag from monocular bounding-box histories.
Established a three-stage curriculum that transitions progressively from privileged control pretraining to estimator training and finally to estimator-based policy fine-tuning.
Combined dodge/recovery and search/track policies on a physical Unitree G1 to demonstrate an 85%+ dodge success rate and repeated evasion loops using only onboard monocular RGB vision.

sections.heading: Why dodgeball for humanoids?
sections.summary: For humanoids to operate in the real world, they must instantly dodge incoming objects and recover while maintaining balance. This work proposes an integrated perception, state estimation, and whole-body control system using only an onboard monocular camera.
sections.details:
Humanoids sharing space with humans need reflexive dodging capabilities to shield themselves from unpredictable incoming or falling objects. Unlike quadrupeds or drones, however, simply moving out of the way is useless for a bipedal robot if it loses balance and tumbles. It requires highly coordinated whole-body motion to dodge while preventing falls, followed by an immediate return to a stable default posture to prepare for subsequent actions.

This study uses dodgeball as a quantitative testbed for this capability. Throws provide clearly controllable speeds, distances, and angles, making it an ideal setup to strictly evaluate the reaction margins available to perception and locomotion.

The hardest part is achieving this solely through a single monocular RGB camera fixed to the robot's torso. Moving the torso to dodge changes the camera's gaze direction dramatically, and vigorous whole-body maneuvers cause severe image shake and blur. Perception and evasion motions strongly interfere with each other.

To address this tight coupling, the authors built a temporal estimator that predicts relative ball positions and threat flags from bounding-box histories, alongside a whole-body control system that composes separately trained dodge/recovery and search/track policies.

captions.F1: Overall system architecture. During simulation training, analytic projection and randomization are used, whereas real-world deployment passes fine-tuned YOLOv8 detections through the temporal estimator into the policy. The design smoothly transitions from privileged training to running entirely on estimated states.

sections.heading: State of the art in agile evasion and humanoid ball sports
sections.summary: Agile evasion of dynamic objects has mostly been studied on drones and quadrupeds, often relying on event cameras. Meanwhile, humanoid ball sports typically depend on external motion capture; this work stands out by achieving whole-body evasion, recovery, and reacquisition using only onboard monocular vision.
sections.details:
### Dynamic obstacle evasion research
In dynamic object evasion for aerial drones, researchers frequently use microsecond-level event cameras alongside standard frame-based sensors to minimize latency and motion blur. Quadrupedal systems like REBot and APREBot have also demonstrated evasion using omnidirectional sensing or active camera setups. However, bipedal robots have a narrow support polygon and a high risk of tipping over, imposing fundamentally different balance constraints compared to quadrupeds or airborne platforms.

### Humanoid ball interactions
For humanoid ball-handling skills, researchers have studied goalkeeper saves and racket sports like table tennis, badminton, and tennis. Yet most prior works rely on external motion capture cameras or marker-instrumented environments in restricted setups.

The closest prior work is PAC-MAN, a humanoid dodgeball system combining control barrier functions (CBF) with adversarial motion priors. However, while PAC-MAN relied on an onboard depth camera with segmentation, this framework uses only a much more accessible and low-cost monocular RGB camera, while extending the capability to full-azimuth search and target reacquisition.

sections.heading: How to catch fast balls and dodge with the whole body using a single camera
sections.summary: The system rests on three pillars: analytic projection to skip simulation rendering, a temporal estimator predicting position and threat flags, and two coordinated policies. A three-stage curriculum ensures stable learning throughout.
sections.details:
### III-A System formulation and task setup
The robot used is a 29-DoF Unitree G1 humanoid. At time step $t$, the perception module outputs a normalized bounding box $\mathbf{b}_t$ (center coordinates, size, and detection flag $m_t$). From this history, the temporal estimator predicts the robot-centric 3D relative ball position $\hat{\mathbf{p}}^r_{b,t}$ and a binary threat flag $\hat{\chi}_t$ indicating whether the ball is incoming. The policy takes these estimates along with proprioceptive states to command target angles across all 29 joints.

In simulation, five throws are launched per episode at random intervals (2–4 seconds). Episodes transition across three phases—rest, launched, and absent—teaching the system to distinguish between visible balls at rest and actual incoming threats that require dodging.

### III-B Fast analytic bounding-box projection
Rendering RGB images for thousands of parallel environments at every RL step incurs massive computational overhead. Exploiting the ball's spherical shape, the authors adopted an analytic projection that computes 2D bounding boxes directly from geometric line-of-sight tangent equations. During physical deployment, a fine-tuned YOLOv8 handles detection; to mimic its imperfections, training injects synthetic detection dropouts, Gaussian noise on box centers, log-normal noise on aspect ratios, and 30–50 ms latency.

### III-C Temporal estimator training
A single monocular frame cannot reveal ball depth or velocity. A 3-layer MLP estimates relative position and threat flags from the bounding-box sequence. Because flight time occupies only a tiny fraction of an episode, naive training tends to bias the model toward predicting non-threat states. To counter this, training uses flight-window sampling and mixes in synthetic rollouts of balls moving slowly or staying stationary within the field of view.

### III-D Whole-body control policy and three-stage curriculum
The control architecture composes two policies: $\pi_{\mathrm{dodge}}$ for collision avoidance and recovery to an upright stance, and $\pi_{\mathrm{search}}$ for full-body yawing to find targets outside the field of view. Switching is handled via detection hysteresis and the threat flag.

Training directly on imperfect estimates from scratch causes the robot to fall constantly, which in turn feeds degraded visual data to the estimator. To avoid this failure loop, the authors designed a three-stage curriculum:
- **Stage 1**: Train whole-body dodging and recovery without falling using ground-truth (GT) ball positions and threat flags.
- **Stage 2**: Once the robot stands reliably (episodes exceeding 900 steps), freeze policy inputs to GT while using the generated visual trajectories to supervise the estimator.
- **Stage 3**: When dodge success surpasses 90%, switch actor inputs from ground truth to estimator outputs, adapting the policy to perception noise and latency.

sections.heading: Achieving 85%+ evasion rate and continuous loops on hardware
sections.summary: Analytic projection sped up observation generation by up to 259x, yielding over 97% dodge success at 5.0 m and 6 m/s in simulation. The physical Unitree G1 exceeded 85% dodging success and performed continuous search-and-dodge cycles on hardware.
sections.details:
### IV-A & IV-B Perception fidelity and massive efficiency gains
Comparing analytic geometric projection against image-based rendering showed that analytic projection maintained a constant step time of ~0.5 ms whether running 1 or 64 parallel environments. By contrast, rendering took 123.67 ms at 32 environments and ran out of GPU memory at 64. Analytic projection accelerated observation generation by 10.2x to 259.7x while dramatically slashing GPU memory consumption.

### IV-C & IV-D Estimator accuracy and curriculum impact
Noise measurements from YOLOv8 outputs on the physical robot matched the simulation's 'low noise' setting (center standard deviation around 2 pixels). In ablation studies, the proposed three-stage curriculum (Full Stages) achieved a 90.8% dodge success rate, whereas training directly on estimator outputs from scratch (Direct Training) degraded performance sharply. This confirms the necessity of establishing solid motor primitives before coupling them with perception.

### IV-E System-level simulation and hardware verification
Rigorous simulation benchmarks (1,000 throws per setting) yielded a 97.8–100.0% dodge success rate at 5.0 m distance and 6 m/s speed. Even under the harshest condition of 2.5 m at 10 m/s—giving a reaction window of merely 0.25 seconds—the system sustained a 33.2–40.8% success rate.

On the physical Unitree G1, running strictly on onboard vision and 50 Hz joint commands without external tracking, the robot achieved an 85%+ success rate (no contact, no fall) across more than 15 controlled single-throw trials. Furthermore, the robot executed a complete hardware sequence: tracking the thrower, dodging a pitch, performing a 360-degree rotation to relocate the thrower who moved out of sight, re-engaging tracking, and dodging a second throw.

captions.F5: Comparison of bounding box generation between analytic projection and rendering. The left plot demonstrates nearly invariant compute time and minimal memory usage across environment counts, while the right table shows high fidelity with sub-pixel center error and IoU exceeding 0.91.
captions.F4: Simulation results across launch speeds (6 m/s, 10 m/s), distances (5.0 m, 2.5 m), and approach angles (left, center, right). Even in high-speed, close-range conditions with only 0.25 s flight time, the robot manages evasive maneuvers while keeping estimator drift bounded.

sections.heading: Conclusion and future outlook
sections.summary: This work presented a monocular evasion and target reacquisition framework for humanoids, validating its efficacy in simulation and on a physical Unitree G1. It lays a groundwork for agile autonomous humanoid behavior under strict sensing and dynamic motion constraints.
sections.details:
By integrating monocular RGB sensing, temporal state estimation, and deep reinforcement learning for whole-body control, this study realized a complete closed-loop system where a humanoid autonomously dodges flying objects, recovers balance, and searches for upcoming threats.

In particular, the high-throughput parallel training via geometric projection and the staged curriculum linking control with estimation proved crucial for tackling dynamic tasks tangled with sensor noise and rapid whole-body motion.

While challenges remain—such as responding to ultra-fast close-range throws and relying on a priori knowledge of ball dimensions—this work marks a significant milestone toward fully untethered, onboard-autonomous humanoid robots.

takeaways: Computing bounding boxes analytically from sphere tangent geometry rather than full rendering speeds up simulation observation generation by over 250x.
In dynamic tasks where control and estimation interlock, a phased curriculum that first secures stable motion using privileged inputs is indispensable.
Even when aggressive evasion shakes the camera view, a single monocular RGB camera can deliver an 85%+ whole-body dodge rate when paired with noise injection and temporal estimation.
limitations: Inferring depth from monocular vision assumes a known physical ball size (radius), which degrades position estimation accuracy for unknown or irregularly sized objects.
The learned evasion policy tends to favor specific dodge directions, indicating that policy distillation or similar methods are needed to promote diverse evasive footwork matched to launch angles.
Rapid torso rotations during the search phase induce motion blur, creating a trade-off where faster scanning increases the risk of missed visual detections.
